opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, especially having moved from research and open-source frameworks into building products and infrastructure for companies.

I'd start with this: listen very carefully to customers, but don't take what they say literally. When a customer tells you, "I need feature X," they're really telling you about a pain point, and feature X is their best guess at a solution, based on what they already know. Your job as a builder is to dig one or two layers deeper. Why do they need it? What were they trying to do when they ran into the problem? Often the real need is something more fundamental, like "my inference cost is too high" or "my engineers spend too much time gluing systems together." The right answer may look quite different from what they first asked for.

Second, I'd separate the needs that are specific to one customer from the needs that show up as a pattern. Early on, especially for a startup, it's tempting to say yes to everything because every customer feels precious. If you build a custom solution for each one, though, you end up as a consulting shop rather than a product company. The skill is to spot the common denominator across many customers and build that really well, so one product serves a hundred people instead of a hundred products serving one person each.

Third, in a fast-moving field like AI, customers' needs change very quickly, sometimes month to month. What people wanted from models two years ago, mostly "does it work at all," is very different from what they want now: reliability, cost efficiency, latency, privacy, integration into real workflows. So you have to stay close to customers continuously, not just do one round of interviews and then disappear for six months to build. Ship something, watch how people actually use it, and iterate.

Finally, I think builders need some conviction of their own. Customers are great at telling you about today's problems. They're less good at telling you what tomorrow's technology makes possible. Part of a builder's job is to combine deep empathy for the customer's pain with your own understanding of where the technology is heading, and sometimes show customers a solution they wouldn't have known to ask for. In my experience, that balance between listening humbly and building with conviction is what separates good products from great ones.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncovering customer pain and building with conviction, but does not address or reject teaching customers to change their behavior.

r002.rationale: It says to listen carefully but not take feature requests literally, and to investigate the underlying pain instead.

r003.rationale: It recommends finding the common denominator across customers and building one product that serves many.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that you have to listen to customers very carefully, but you can't just build what they literally ask for. When I was working on Caffe and later on the AI infrastructure at Facebook and Alibaba, the requests we got were almost always framed in terms of the problem the person was staring at that day: make this model train faster, support this one operator, give me a button for this. If you take every one of those at face value, you end up with a product that's a pile of features and no coherent shape.

So the discipline I try to follow is to ask "why" a couple of levels down. A customer says they want lower latency. Why? Because their cost per request is too high. Why does that matter? Because they're trying to run inference at a scale where the economics only work if it's an order of magnitude cheaper. Now you're solving a real problem, and the solution might not be the thing they asked for at all. It might be a different serving architecture, or batching, or a quantization path they didn't know existed. Half of building infrastructure is translating between what people say and what they actually need.

The second thing is that there's a difference between the loud customer and the representative customer. The person who files the most detailed issue is giving you a gift, but they may also be an outlier. You have to look across many users and find the pattern. When many different people are hacking around the same limitation in slightly different ways, that's the signal. That's where you should invest.

And then I'd say: move fast on the response, even if you're slow on the final design. Customers forgive a lot if they feel heard. A quick acknowledgment, a workaround, a clear "here's where this fits in our plan" buys you time to do the thing properly. What they don't forgive is silence, or being told "that's not how we think about it." In open source especially, the community is the product. The way you respond to people is as much the product as the code.

So, in short: listen for the underlying problem, look for the pattern rather than the loudest voice, respond quickly, and reserve the right to solve it differently than it was asked. The customers who end up most loyal are usually the ones who got something better than what they originally wanted.

r001.rationale: The response advises interpreting requests differently, but it does not address or reject teaching customers to change their behavior.

r002.rationale: It says to listen carefully without building every literal request, and to uncover the underlying problem instead.

r003.rationale: It recommends finding patterns across users and gives alternative technical approaches, but does not clearly state that builders should distill needs into a scalable solution.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is to understand what the customer is trying to accomplish. Customers will often come to you with a specific feature request, but that request is already a proposed solution. As a product builder, you need to ask: What problem led you to ask for this? What are you doing today, and where does it become difficult?

That doesn’t mean you dismiss what they’re asking for. You listen carefully, then work with them to see whether your solution actually helps. Sometimes the right answer is exactly the feature they requested. Sometimes a much simpler change solves the underlying problem.

The other challenge is finding what’s common across those conversations. You can’t build a separate product for every customer. You want to respond to individual needs while developing something that helps a broader group of people. That takes judgment, and it takes repeatedly putting the product in customers’ hands and learning from how they use it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses understanding customer problems and evaluating solutions, but does not reject teaching customers to change their behavior.

r002.rationale: It says to listen carefully without dismissing requests, while treating them as proposed solutions and checking whether they address the underlying problem.

r003.rationale: It says to find what customers’ conversations have in common, since builders cannot make a separate product for every customer, and to develop something that helps a broader group.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first step is to understand the problem behind the request. A customer might ask for a particular feature, but that feature is their proposed solution. As a product builder, you need to ask: What are you trying to accomplish? What is difficult about doing that today?

Then you have to look for patterns. If several customers are struggling with the same underlying problem, that can point to something you should build into the product. You still need judgment—you can’t turn every request into a roadmap item. But you should listen carefully, build something that addresses the need, and go back to the customer to see whether it actually helps. That feedback loop is really important.

r001.rationale: The response says to understand customers’ underlying problems and build something helpful, but it does not reject teaching customers to change their behavior.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes a customer’s requested feature from the underlying need and says not to turn every request into a roadmap item.

r003.rationale: It recommends looking for patterns across customers with the same underlying problem and building that need into the product, which communicates a product-level solution.
